title: Feeding by Tourists Puts Japan's Rabbit Island at Risk
paragraphs: For rabbit fans, Okunoshima might sound like heaven. The small, uninhabited Japanese island is home to hundreds of free-roaming rabbits, with visitors coming from around the world to get up close and feed them.
But recently, some much less cuddly animals have been joining them — wild boars.
Okunoshima, around 60 kilometers east of Hiroshima City, is better known as "Rabbit Island." Hundreds of thousands of people come to the island each year to see its famous residents.

Rabbits have lived on Okunoshima for decades, despite not being native to the island. While it's not clear where the rabbits came from, one report from a local newspaper in 1972 said a nearby elementary school released a group of them on the island.
Today, the large rabbit population depends heavily on tourists. Visitors regularly bring food for the rabbits, supporting far more of them than the island could naturally feed.
But the rabbits aren't the only ones getting those free meals.
A recent study found that native wild boars have been eating food left for the rabbits. They've also been seen eating dead rabbits and even attacking live ones.
In March 2024, a wild boar was seen catching a live rabbit near a tourist area. A similar attack was reported in 2017.
Researchers say this is unusual, as wild boars aren't generally known for hunting live animals.
The rabbits are causing problems of their own, too. With so many looking for food, they've eaten large amounts of the island's plants.

Researchers say feeding by tourists may be playing a part in both problems. The feeding supports a rabbit population larger than the island can naturally hold, while leftover food may attract wild boars to areas where rabbits live.
Researchers have suggested stricter feeding rules, and keeping a closer eye on rabbit numbers and the island's plants.
Okunoshima might look like heaven for rabbit lovers, but keeping it that way is becoming a little more complicated.
